meaning: Look closely at the parts of a media text and explain how they create meaning.
example: We will analyse the front cover of the magazine.
note: analyse = verb, analysis = noun. British spelling: analyse.

meaning: A close, detailed study of how something creates meaning.
example: Her analysis of the poster focuses on colour and lighting.
note: We write 'an analysis of' something.

meaning: What you say or write in reply to a question.
example: Use evidence from the image in your answer.

meaning: Look at how two or more things are similar and different.
example: Compare the two adverts and their target audiences.
note: compare A with B. Write about both things.

meaning: Show the differences between things; a clear difference.
example: There is a strong contrast between the dark background and the bright face.
note: a contrast between A and B.

meaning: Say what you can see or what something is like.
example: Describe the setting of the advert.
note: Describe = what you see. Explain = why it matters.

meaning: A small part or fact that you notice.
example: One small detail is the ring on her finger.

meaning: The result a choice has on the audience.
example: The close-up has a powerful effect on the audience.
note: have an effect on someone. The verb is 'affect'.

meaning: Details from the text that prove your point.
example: The bright smile is evidence that she is happy.
note: Uncountable: 'evidence', never 'evidences'.

meaning: One thing that shows what you mean.
example: For example, the man is wearing an expensive suit.

meaning: Say why or how something happens or creates meaning.
example: Explain why the advert uses a close-up.
note: Explain = give reasons. Use 'because' or 'this suggests that'.

meaning: Name or point out something.
example: Identify two creative choices in the poster.

meaning: A thought or message.
example: The advert sells the idea that the family is happy.

meaning: What something expresses or tells the audience.
example: The colour red adds meaning to the image.

meaning: The reason a media text was made; what it wants to do.
example: The purpose of the advert is to sell the perfume.
note: the purpose of something; 'to sell', 'to inform', 'to persuade'.

meaning: Why something happens or is done.
example: One reason for this choice is to attract young people.
note: the reason for + noun.

meaning: How someone reacts to a media text.
example: The audience's response may be sympathy.

meaning: Give evidence to show a point is true.
example: Use details from the image to support your point.

meaning: A decision the producer makes about how to create the text.
example: The choice of a city setting suggests a modern lifestyle.

meaning: The people who see, read or listen to a media text.
example: The audience can see the woman's facial expression clearly.

meaning: The particular group a media text is made for.
example: The target audience is probably teenagers.
note: The advert is aimed at teenagers. The target audience is teenagers.

meaning: How people, places or ideas are shown in the media.
example: The poster offers a positive representation of older people.
similar: represent; present; show; stereotype; stereotypical; positive; negative
note: a representation of a group. It is always a choice, never just 'reality'.

meaning: Show a person, group or idea in a particular way.
example: The magazine tends to represent women as caring.
note: represent someone as + adjective: 'represents him as strong'.

meaning: A simple, fixed idea about what a group of people is like.
example: The advert uses the stereotype of the perfect housewife.
similar: represent; representation; present; show; stereotypical; traditional

meaning: Showing a group in a simple, fixed and expected way.
example: The boy is shown in a stereotypical way, playing football.
similar: represent; representation; present; show; stereotype; traditional

meaning: Following ideas or roles that have existed for a long time.
example: The family is shown in traditional roles.

meaning: Normal and not special.
example: The model looks like an ordinary person, not a celebrity.

meaning: Normal and part of daily life.
example: The advert shows an everyday kitchen.
note: everyday (adjective) = normal. every day (two words) = each day.

meaning: Showing someone or something in a good way.
example: This is a positive representation of teenagers.

meaning: Showing someone or something in a bad way.
example: News stories often give a negative view of young people.

meaning: Close to real life.
example: The family looks realistic because the house is messy.

meaning: Who a person is, or the groups they feel they belong to.
example: Her clothing shows her identity as a sports fan.

meaning: The position or job a person has in a situation.
example: The father has the role of the protector.

meaning: A number of people who share something, such as age or gender.
example: The advert represents older people as a group.

meaning: One person, seen separately from a group.
example: The poster shows each athlete as an individual.

meaning: Make something clear or visible.
example: The bright colours show that the product is fun.
similar: represent; representation; present; stereotype; stereotypical; communicate; create

meaning: Make the audience think of an idea without saying it directly.
example: The dark lighting may suggest danger.
note: suggest that + sentence, or suggest + noun.

meaning: Express an idea indirectly, so the audience has to work it out.
example: Her smile seems to imply that she is happy with the product.
note: The text implies; the audience infers.

meaning: Show someone or something in a particular way.
example: The article tries to present the team as heroes.
similar: represent; representation; show; stereotype; stereotypical; communicate; create
note: present someone as + noun or adjective.

meaning: Make a mood, feeling or meaning.
example: The music and lighting create a tense mood.

meaning: Question or go against a usual idea or stereotype.
example: This advert tries to challenge the stereotype that girls are weak.
note: challenge a stereotype = go against it.

meaning: Make an existing idea or stereotype stronger.
example: Images like this reinforce the idea that men should be strong.
note: reinforce = make stronger. The opposite of challenge.

meaning: Pass a message or feeling to the audience.
example: Her body language helps to communicate confidence.
similar: meaning; idea; show; present; create; suggest; imply

meaning: A picture, such as a photograph or drawing.
example: The main image shows a family on a beach.

meaning: The device used to take photographs or film.
example: The photographer uses a camera to take the picture.

meaning: The position the camera looks from: above, below or at eye level.
example: The camera angle makes the man look powerful.

meaning: A shot taken very near, often showing a face or a small detail.
example: A close-up of her face shows that she is worried.

meaning: The part of an image that is behind the main subject.
example: In the background, there is a busy city.

meaning: The part of an image nearest to the audience, at the front.
example: In the foreground, a girl is holding a trophy.

meaning: Where and when the image or scene takes place.
example: The setting is a modern office.

meaning: The clothes chosen for a character or model.
example: The superhero's costume is red and blue.

meaning: Clothes in general.
example: His smart clothing suggests he is professional.
note: Uncountable: 'clothing', not 'clothings'.

meaning: The way a person stands or sits for a photo.
example: Her pose, with hands on hips, looks confident.

meaning: The look on someone's face that shows feeling.
example: His facial expression is serious.

meaning: How a person's body position and movement show feelings.
example: Her open body language makes her look friendly.

meaning: Red, blue, green and so on; colours can carry meaning.
example: The colour gold suggests wealth.
note: British spelling: colour. American: color.

meaning: How light is used in an image: bright, dark, soft or harsh.
example: Bright lighting makes the scene look happy.

meaning: A short, memorable phrase used in an advert.
example: The slogan is 'Just do it'.

meaning: The title of a news story, printed in large letters.
example: The headline describes the players as heroes.

meaning: The words a media text uses and how they are chosen.
example: The advert uses positive language such as 'amazing'.

meaning: Sure of yourself and your abilities.
example: She looks confident because she is smiling at the camera.

meaning: Physically powerful, or not easily upset.
example: The athlete is represented as strong.

meaning: Not strong; easily hurt or beaten.
example: Older people are sometimes shown as weak.

meaning: Having a lot of control or influence.
example: The low camera position makes the leader look powerful.
similar: strong; confident; independent; wealthy; successful; professional

meaning: Having achieved what you wanted, such as money or fame.
example: The businessman is presented as successful.

meaning: Kind and showing that you want to help others.
example: The nurse is represented as caring and gentle.

meaning: Kind and pleasant to other people.
example: His wide smile makes him look friendly.

meaning: Not smiling or joking; thinking about important things.
example: The doctor has a serious facial expression.

meaning: Looking skilled, smart and good at a job.
example: Her suit makes her look professional.

meaning: Good-looking or pleasant to look at.
example: The models are young and attractive.

meaning: New and up to date.
example: The family lives in a modern house.

meaning: Having a lot of money.
example: The gold watch suggests he is wealthy.

meaning: Easily hurt and needing protection.
example: The child looks small and vulnerable in the dark street.

meaning: Not needing help or control from other people.
example: The woman is represented as independent because she travels alone.

meaning: Sensible and able to be trusted to look after things.
example: The older brother is shown as responsible.

meaning: A picture, film or text that tries to make people buy something or support an idea.
example: The advert for the new trainers shows a runner crossing a finish line at dawn.

meaning: A large printed picture with a few words, put up on a wall to tell people about something.
example: The poster for the school play shows a single red mask on a black background.

meaning: The front page of a magazine, with its main picture, its title and the stories inside.
example: This month's magazine cover shows a tennis player laughing in the rain.

meaning: A small design that a company or group uses so that people recognise it.
example: The café's logo is a steaming cup drawn with one curly line.

meaning: A few words printed under or next to a photo to say what it shows.
example: The caption under the photo says "Head teacher opens new library".

meaning: An object a person holds or uses in a photo or scene to add meaning.
example: The scientist in the poster holds a test tube: one prop tells us her job straight away.

meaning: A person in a story, film, advert or game.
example: The main character in the advert is a grandmother who learns to skateboard.

meaning: A shot taken from above, looking down, which can make someone look small or weak.
example: A high angle shows the lost boy sitting alone on a huge station floor.

meaning: A shot taken from below, looking up, which can make someone look strong or important.
example: The low angle makes the young captain tower over the camera.

meaning: Taken from the same height as a person's eyes, so the viewer meets them as an equal.
example: The interview is filmed at eye-level, so the nurse seems calm and easy to talk to.

meaning: A shot that shows a whole person and a lot of the place around them.
example: A long shot shows the farmer standing alone in an empty field.

meaning: A shot that shows a person from the waist up.
example: The newsreader is filmed in a mid shot, so we see her face and her hands on the desk.

meaning: The part of an image that is sharp and clear, while other parts may be blurred.
example: The focus is on the girl's hands; the crowd behind her is just a blur.

meaning: A movement of the hand, arm or head that shows a feeling or an idea.
example: Her thumbs-up is a simple gesture that tells the audience the product works.

meaning: The real place where a photo is taken or a scene is filmed.
example: The advert's location is a real fishing village, not a studio.

meaning: An object, colour or picture that stands for an idea.
example: A white dove in the poster is a symbol of peace.

meaning: People who share something, such as age, gender, job, religion or where they live.
example: The magazine represents teenagers as a social group that only cares about phones.

meaning: A person who watches a film, TV programme, video or image.
example: The final scene leaves every viewer wondering who sent the letter.

meaning: Build a representation on purpose by choosing and arranging details.
example: The photographer constructs a calm, happy family with a sunny garden and matching jumpers.

meaning: A representation built from chosen details, not simply a copy of real life.
example: The "perfect morning" in the cereal advert is a construction: the light, the kitchen and every smile were planned.

meaning: A statement that says something is true of everyone in a group when it is only true of some.
example: "Teenagers never read" is a generalisation that the article never tries to prove.

meaning: A fixed, simple idea about what men or women are like or should do.
example: Tool kits for boys and tea sets for girls: the toy catalogue repeats a gender stereotype.

meaning: A fixed, simple idea about what people of a certain age are like.
example: The sitcom's grandad, confused by every phone, is a tired age stereotype.

meaning: A fixed, simple idea about people from a particular country, culture or religion.
example: The film's only French character wears a beret and carries a baguette, a lazy cultural stereotype.

meaning: Showing a person or group in a good way, with qualities the audience will admire.
example: The documentary gives a positive representation of young carers as patient, organised and funny.

meaning: Showing a person or group in a bad way, so the audience thinks less of them.
example: Headlines that mention young people only when there is trouble create a negative representation.

meaning: Including people of many different backgrounds, ages, bodies and abilities.
example: The sports brand shows its diversity with athletes in wheelchairs, in hijabs and in school kit.

meaning: Favouring one side or group unfairly, so a representation is not balanced.
example: The report shows bias: it quotes six fans of the new road and none of the people who live beside it.

meaning: What the edges of a shot include or leave out, and where people are placed inside them.
example: Tight framing squeezes the family into one corner of the picture, so their flat feels crowded.

meaning: How everything in an image is arranged: where people, objects and empty space are placed.
example: The composition puts the winner in the centre and her rivals at the dark edges.

meaning: The set of colours chosen for an image, film or design.
example: The horror film's colour palette is grey, green and a single bright red.

meaning: Soft yellow, orange or golden light that makes a scene feel safe, happy or cosy.
example: Warm lighting from the fireplace makes the grandparents' kitchen feel welcoming.

meaning: Blue, white or grey light that makes a scene feel lonely, tense or unfriendly.
example: Cold lighting in the hospital corridor makes the waiting father look even more alone.

meaning: The use of objects, colours or images to stand for bigger ideas.
example: The symbolism of the broken clock suggests that the family is stuck in the past.

meaning: An idea or feeling that a word, colour or image suggests, beyond what it literally shows.
example: Red has connotations of danger, but also of love.

meaning: What an image or word simply shows or says, before we think about what it suggests.
example: The literal meaning of the photo is a man holding an umbrella; it suggests he is prepared for anything.

meaning: An idea a text suggests without saying it, which the audience has to work out.
example: The empty fridge in the last shot carries an implied meaning: the family cannot afford food.

meaning: When a person in a media text looks or speaks straight at the audience.
example: The footballer stares into the camera, and his direct address makes the viewer feel personally challenged.

meaning: Words chosen to make the audience feel strongly, such as anger, pity or excitement.
example: "Abandoned, shivering puppies" is the emotive language that opens the charity's appeal.

meaning: The particular words a writer chooses, and the effect those words have.
example: Calling the striking workers "heroes" rather than "troublemakers" is a deliberate word choice.

meaning: Using the same word, image or idea more than once to make it stick.
example: The repetition of "every child" makes the promise in the speech sound bigger each time.

meaning: A usual way of doing something in a type of media text, which audiences expect.
example: A large headline across the top is a convention of newspaper front pages.

meaning: A person who buys or uses products and services, or who uses media.
example: The phone company sees every teenager as a future consumer.

meaning: Attract or interest a particular audience.
example: The bright, fast cartoon style is designed to appeal to young children.

meaning: Catch the audience's attention and keep them interested or involved.
example: The quiz at the end of each episode engages viewers who might otherwise switch off.

meaning: Feel that you are like a character and share their feelings or situation.
example: Many first-year students identify with the nervous boy on his first day.

meaning: How the audience thinks, feels or acts because of a media text.
example: The intended audience response to the road-safety film is shock, then a promise to slow down.

meaning: Shown as perfect, better than anyone or anything could really be.
example: The cooking show presents an idealised mother who never looks tired and never burns anything.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Easy for the audience to understand and recognise from their own lives.
example: The vlogger's messy bedroom and missed homework make her relatable to her fans.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Showing a life the audience would like to have, to make them want something.
example: The holiday advert is aspirational: an empty white beach, a private pool and no queues.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: The most common way a group is shown in the media, which can start to seem normal.
example: The dominant representation of scientists is still an older man in a white coat.

meaning: A way of showing a group that differs from the usual, most common one.
example: The series offers an alternative representation of farmers: young, online and running their own businesses.

meaning: A representation that deliberately goes against the usual fixed idea about a group.
example: An older woman running a tech company is a counter-stereotype in the laptop advert.

meaning: Shown less often in the media than the group's real numbers would suggest.
example: Disabled people are under-represented in fashion adverts.

meaning: Shown more often in the media than the group's real numbers would suggest.
example: Young men are over-represented in news stories about crime.

meaning: Showing only some of the details and leaving others out, on purpose.
example: The holiday brochure is selective: it shows the beach but not the motorway behind the hotel.

meaning: Passed to the audience through someone else's choices, so it is never reality itself.
example: Even live news is mediated: someone decides where the cameras point.

meaning: Make something seem normal and acceptable by showing it again and again.
example: Endless jokes about the "useless dad" normalise the idea that fathers can't cook.

meaning: Including one person from a group only to look fair, without giving them a real role.
example: Putting one woman on the poster but giving her no lines in the film is tokenism.

meaning: The way a text leads the audience to take a particular view of the people or events in it.
example: Through audience positioning, the documentary makes us see the factory owner through his workers' eyes.

meaning: The idea that people think about media texts and decide for themselves what they mean.
example: As an active audience, the class argues about whether the advert is funny or insulting.

meaning: The idea that people simply accept what media texts tell them, without questioning it.
example: Critics of the game treat young players as a passive audience who will copy whatever they see.

meaning: How a media text is received and understood by different audiences.
example: The film's reception was warm in cinemas but angry on social media.

meaning: The way a media text speaks to its audience, for example friendly, formal or bossy.
example: The magazine's chatty mode of address, full of "you" and jokes, feels like a friend talking.

meaning: Based on personal feelings and opinions rather than facts.
example: Calling the singer "the voice of a generation" is subjective: nobody can check it.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Based on facts and not influenced by personal feelings.
example: The report tries to be objective by giving both sides the same amount of space.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: The way words, such as a caption or slogan, fix one meaning of an image for the audience.
example: Without the caption "Hero of the flood", the photo of the muddy man could mean anything: the words provide anchorage.
zh: 锚定（文字固定图像意义）

meaning: Everything placed in front of the camera: setting, props, costume, lighting and how people stand and move.
example: The mise-en-scène of the detective's office, with piles of files and a forgotten coffee, shows how hard he works.

meaning: Real and true to life, not faked or performed for the camera.
example: The advert feels authentic because real customers, not actors, tell their own stories.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Clearly made or arranged, so it does not seem natural or real.
example: The smiles in the stock photo look artificial: nobody laughs that hard at a spreadsheet.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Made bigger, stronger or more extreme than it really is.
example: The cartoon villain's exaggerated laugh tells young viewers at once that he is bad.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Made simpler than it really is, so important differences are lost.
example: The quiz show offers a simplified picture of "nerds": glasses, maths and nothing else.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Following the usual, expected way of doing things.
example: The perfume advert is conventional: a beautiful couple, a beach and a slow-motion kiss.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Different from the usual, expected way of doing things.
example: In an unconventional choice, the fashion magazine puts a farmer, not a film star, on its cover.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: A set of beliefs and values about how society is or should be, which a text may support or question.
example: The car advert carries an ideology of success: a bigger car means a better life.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: Pushed to the edge of society or of a story, with little power or attention.
example: Homeless people are marginalised in the drama, seen only in the background of street scenes.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: Representing a group as strange or different from "us", so they seem not to belong.
example: Calling migrants "a flood" is othering: it turns people into a threat from outside.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: Two ideas set up as opposites, such as good and evil or city and country, which a text uses to create meaning.
example: The poster sets up a binary opposition between the bright, busy city and the dark, empty countryside.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: The mixing of two or more cultures to create something new.
example: The music video celebrates cultural hybridity: a Cantonese rap over a Scottish fiddle, like the singer's own family.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: When a text can be read in more than one way and does not settle on one meaning.
example: The ambiguity of the final shot, an open door at night, leaves us unsure whether she has escaped.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: Turn an expected idea upside down, often to make the audience question it.
example: The advert subverts the fairy tale: the princess climbs the tower to rescue the prince.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: The idea that a person's identities, such as race, gender and class, combine and shape their experience together.
example: Intersectionality helps explain why older Black women are almost never the lead in the show.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: When the camera shows women as objects to be looked at, as if from a man's point of view.
example: The camera lingers on the singer's body rather than her face, a clear example of the male gaze.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: The meaning the producer wants the audience to take from a text.
example: The preferred reading of the anti-smoking poster is simple: never start.

meaning: A response that accepts part of a text's intended message but rejects or changes another part.
example: She admires the watch advert's style but laughs at its promise of happiness: a negotiated reading.

meaning: A response that rejects the meaning the producer intended.
example: Seeing the army recruitment advert as a warning against joining up is an oppositional reading.

meaning: How producers build meanings into a text through their choices.
example: Through careful encoding, the election poster puts the candidate in sunlight and his rival in shadow.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: How audiences work out meanings from a text, which may not be what the producer intended.
example: Decoding depends on the audience: a farmer and a city student may read the same tractor advert very differently.
group: Ideology and theory 意识形态与理论

meaning: Showing small but important differences, so a person or issue is not simply good or bad.
example: The film gives a nuanced picture of the bully: cruel at school, but frightened at home.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Containing ideas that go against each other.
example: The magazine sends contradictory messages: "love your body" on one page, a diet plan on the next.
group: Judging a representation 评价再现

meaning: Giving help and encouragement to other people.
example: The supportive coach kneels beside the girl who has just fallen.

meaning: Looking relaxed and real, not posed or made up.
example: In the school brochure the pupils look natural, laughing between lessons rather than posing.

meaning: Having small faults or marks, as real people do.
example: The skincare advert shows imperfect skin, freckles and all.

meaning: Able to do things well without help.
example: The young mechanic is shown as capable: she fixes the engine while the men watch.

meaning: Refusing to give up, even when something is difficult.
example: Soaked and limping, the determined runner keeps going in the final mile.

meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to.
example: Sitting on the patient's side of the desk makes the doctor in the poster look approachable.

meaning: Able to be trusted to be honest and to do the right thing.
example: Bank adverts often use calm, grey-haired presenters to seem trustworthy.

meaning: Wanting very much to succeed or to achieve something big.
example: The ambitious student in the drama stays in the library long after everyone else has gone home.

meaning: Good at something because of training or practice.
example: Close-ups of the potter's fast, steady hands show how skilled he is.

meaning: Attractive in an exciting, expensive and fashionable way.
example: The glamorous film star steps out of the car into a wall of camera flashes.

meaning: Needing someone else's help or money to live or cope.
example: The old advert shows the wife as dependent, asking her husband for money for a new oven.

meaning: Seeming to know a lot and to be in charge, so people listen.
example: Filmed in front of a wall of books, the professor sounds authoritative.

meaning: Looking perfect and carefully prepared, with nothing out of place.
example: The influencer's polished photos hide the hours spent getting each one exactly right.

meaning: Something many people would want to have or to be like.
example: Putting the watch on a famous sailor's wrist makes it desirable.
zh: 令人向往的；有吸引力的

meaning: Caring for others and helping them to grow and develop.
example: The grandfather is shown as nurturing as he teaches his grandson to plant seeds.
